newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Portugal/Germany bond spread may widen to 160 bps.
newsitem.headline: Portugal/Germany bond spread may widen to 160 bps.

text.p: A flight out of southern European bond markets triggered by single currency fears could send the spread between the benchmark Portuguese cash bond and the German Bund to 160 basis points, where it should find good support, analysts and traders said.
Some analysts said that expectations for aggressive rate cuts by the Bank of Portugal, which had encouraged the market at the start of the year, had been effectively crushed by the sell-off.

The March futures contract was down 137 basis points at 106.84 on Friday, close to key support at 106.50, while the spread between the February 2007 cash bond and the Bund equivalent stood at 135 basis points against 117 on Thursday night.
The spread had narrowed to a record 83 basis points in January when single currency optimism was at its height.
The spread with Germany was last above 140 in November 1996.
"Very short-term, the spread could fluctuate between current levels close to 140 and 160," said Mario Vigario of Deutsche Morgan Grennfell in Lisbon.
"I believe that the spread could widen due to the pessimism over monetary union and could go quickly to 160 basis points before recovering a bit," said analyst Martin Amaral Neto of Banco ESSI.
"A spread of 160 bps would be compatible with a negative spread of 10 to 20 with Spain," said a trader at a large bank.

Nervousness had intensified on Friday after Bundesbank board member Peter Schmidhuber said that countries wanting to join the single currency must have a good track record of stability and a final sprint to the 1997 finish was not good enough.
The remarks were seen aimed primarily at Italy, but Spain and Portugal were also caught by the shockwave.

"Confidence is being lost that Portugal will be in monetary union in 1999. The chances were drastically reduced for political reasons and not for fundamental reasons," said an analyst with a foreign bank.
"Divergence trades are beginning to replace convergence trades," said Amaral Neto.
The idea that the Bank of Portugal would no longer have as much room to cut rates would hit the middle and short end of the curve hardest, analysts said.
"All the curve is under pressure but the short and medium sector could fall most," said an analyst at one large national bank.

Amaral Neto said that he had been forecasting a Bank of Portugal repo rate around 5.30 percent at the end of the year but the Forward Rate Agreement market was pointing to a repo of around 5.80 percent.
